arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Bendure argued that Rule 15(c)(1)(C) permits adding new defendants after the limitations period expires.
Mr. Glazier argued that a plaintiff's knowledge of the proper party's identity can preclude a finding of mistake.
Justice Scalia questioned why a plaintiff would not read the contract carefully before filing suit.
Justice Roberts clarified that the issue involves the real name of the party who caused the injury.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of Federal Rule 15(c)(1)(C). The rule allows adding new defendants after the limitations period ends. The core issue is whether a plaintiff's prior knowledge of the correct party's identity blocks this amendment.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to allow the amendment. They argue knowledge of the correct party does not preclude relation back.
the opposing side wants the Court to deny the amendment. They argue the plaintiff knew the correct party and thus made no mistake.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case contends that a plaintiff's knowledge about the proper party's identity does not preclude a finding of mistake.
the opposing side contends that the ticket clearly identified the proper party, so no mistake occurred.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the limits of amending complaints. It determines when plaintiffs can add parties after deadlines. It affects access to courts for injured parties. It clarifies the standard for mistake in identity.
